title: Unit 1 Checkpoint Review
goal: I can use what I learned in Weeks 1 to 4, in math and reading, to get ready for my Checkpoint.

card.desc: A review lesson with no new skill. Ce'Line retells Theo's trail stories and reviews all of Unit 1 (Pathways Weeks 1–4): place value and rounding, comparing and ordering, adding and subtracting with regrouping, and word problems with estimates, plus character and setting, conflict, sequence and theme. It gets her ready for the Pathways Unit 1 Checkpoint (Week 5).

win: You reviewed all of Unit 1. You are ready for the Checkpoint!

slides.title: Checkpoint Review Day
slides.text: Today we look back at Weeks 1 to 4. No new skill today! We review math and reading. Then you will be ready for your Checkpoint.

notes.do: Before class: look at her Lesson 4 Show What You Know score (Formspree) and any Pathways Week 1–4 retake scores. Write the weakest week on a sticky note for yourself. Set out the whiteboard, two marker colors, 6 index cards, a highlighter and pencil and paper.
notes.say: Today is a review day. Everything today is something you already learned. You know more than you think!
notes.ask: What is one thing you remember from our lessons so far, math or reading?
notes.listen: Any real answer. Praise it and write it in the corner of the whiteboard. She needs a confident start.

slides.title: Theo's trail stories
slides.text: All month, you read about Theo. Tell me his stories in your own words.
prompts: Who is Theo? Where did his first hike take place?
What was Theo's problem when the trail split in two?
How did he fix it? Where did he end up?
What did his family do first at the campsite?
What did Theo do with the last marshmallow? Why?

notes.do: 7 minutes. She tells it first, no help. Then ask the prompts she skipped. Draw a simple trail on the whiteboard with 4 stops: Hike, Missing Sign, Camping, Marshmallow. Add one word at each stop as she talks.
notes.say: The Checkpoint asks about Theo's stories. Let's remember them together.
notes.ask: Who gave Theo the compass? Who told him about the valley view?
notes.listen: His father gave him the old brass compass. His grandfather used to describe the view. The sign was gone and the trail split; he used the compass and map, went right (the open rock path) and reached Lookout Peak. Camping: tent first, then fire, then chili, last the stars. Marshmallow: he broke it in half and gave Mia the bigger piece. If she mixes up the stories, point to the trail stops.

slides.title: What the Checkpoint checks
slides.text: The Checkpoint has math and reading from Weeks 1 to 4.

visual.text: 4 weeks · 8 skills

steps.text: Week 1: place value and rounding · character and setting.
Week 2: comparing and ordering numbers · conflict, attempt and resolution.
Week 3: adding and subtracting with regrouping · sequence: beginning, middle, end.
Week 4: word problems and estimating · theme, the lesson of a story.

slides.tip: On the Checkpoint you get 2 tries. Only your first try earns points. So slow down and work on paper first.

notes.do: Read each step with her. Let her tap to show the next one.
notes.say: There is nothing new today. Today is about getting each one right on the FIRST try.
notes.ask: Which week feels easiest for you? Which one feels hardest?
notes.listen: Write her hardest week on the whiteboard. Spend one extra minute there today.

slides.title: Six Checkpoint words
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: What a digit is worth because of where it sits in a number.
words.example: In 862, the 8 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 800.

words.meaning: To trade 10 of one place for 1 of the next place.
A close guess. You round the numbers first.
The problem a character has in a story.
words.example: Zuri's kite is stuck in a tree. That is the conflict.

words.meaning: The order that things happen in.
words.example: First, next, then and last show the sequence.

words.meaning: The lesson or big idea a story teaches.
words.example: Zuri's story theme: stay calm and think when you have a problem.

notes.do: She reads each card out loud. Then she covers it and says the meaning in her own words. She writes each word on the front of an index card. She finishes the backs at home.
notes.say: These six words are on the Checkpoint. Three are math words. Three are reading words.
notes.ask: Which word means the order things happen in?
notes.listen: Sequence. If she says theme, read both cards again: theme is the lesson, sequence is the order.

slides.title: Place value and rounding
slides.text: Every digit has a place. Its place tells what it is worth.

steps.text: In 862, the 8 is worth 800. The 6 is worth 60. The 2 is worth 2.
Expanded form: 862 = 800 + 60 + 2.
Round to the nearest ten: look at the ones digit. 862 → the 2 is 4 or less → 860.
Round to the nearest hundred: look at the tens digit. 862 → the 6 is 5 or more → 900.

slides.tip: 5 or more? Round up. 4 or less? Round down.

notes.do: Write 862 on the whiteboard in a place value chart. She points to each digit and says what it is worth.
notes.ask: For the nearest hundred, which digit do we look at?
notes.listen: The tens digit (the one to the RIGHT of the hundreds). A common mistake is looking at the ones digit. Point to the place you are rounding to, then the digit just to its right.

slides.title: Week 1 on paper
slides.text: Write it on paper first. Then type.

items.q: In 491, what is the 9 worth?
items.why: The 9 is in the tens place. 9 tens = 90.
items.no: Find the place. Is the 9 in the hundreds, tens or ones?
items.hint: The 4 is worth 400. The 9 comes next.

items.q: Write 705 in expanded form: 705 = ____
items.why: 7 hundreds and 5 ones. The 0 tens is worth 0. 700 + 5 (or 700 + 0 + 5).
items.no: Write what each digit is worth, with plus signs.

items.q: Round 765 to the nearest hundred: ____
items.why: 765 is between 700 and 800. Look at the tens digit: 6. That is 5 or more, so round up. 800
items.no: Look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: 765 is between 700 and 800. Which one is it closer to?

notes.do: Paper first. She says the place out loud before she types.
notes.listen: The 7 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 700. The 0 holds the tens place.

slides.title: Compare and order
slides.text: Start with the biggest place. If it ties, move to the next place.

visual.sub: Hundreds tie. Tens: 4 is less than 6.

steps.text: 746 and 764. Hundreds: 7 and 7. A tie! Keep going.
Tens: 4 and 6. 6 is bigger. So 746 < 764.
> means greater than. < means less than. The open side faces the bigger number.
Order 391, 319, 913 from least to greatest: 319, 391, 913.
In a race, the smallest time wins. Smallest time = fastest.

slides.tip: Read the question. Does it want least first, or greatest first?

notes.do: Write 746 and 764 on the whiteboard, one on top of the other. She circles the first place where they are different.
notes.ask: Which way does the open side of < face?
notes.listen: Toward the bigger number. If she mixes them up, draw a mouth that wants to eat the bigger number.

slides.title: Week 2 on paper
slides.text: Line the numbers up on paper. Then type.

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 0 and 8. 8 is bigger, so 580 is bigger. 508 < 580 means 508 is less than 580. <
items.no: Start with the hundreds. If they tie, look at the tens. The open side faces the bigger number.
items.hint: The point of the sign touches the smaller number.

items.q:
Put these in order from greatest to least: 547, 574, 457.
Type them with commas: ____
items.why: Compare the hundreds first. If two tie, compare the tens. From greatest to least: 574, 547, 457
items.no: Look at the hundreds digits first. If two numbers have the same hundreds digit, look at the tens.

items.q: Hana ran 214 seconds. Rafi ran 241 seconds. Cara ran 209 seconds. Who was fastest? Type the name.
items.why: In a race, the smallest time wins. 209 is the smallest. Cara was fastest.
items.no: Fastest means the SMALLEST time.
items.hint: All three have 2 hundreds. Look at the tens.

notes.do: She writes the numbers in a column on paper, lined up by place.
notes.ask: Why is the smallest number the winner in a race?
notes.listen: A smaller time means it took less time, so that runner finished first.

slides.title: Add with regrouping
slides.text: Add the ones first. If a column makes 10 or more, regroup.

steps.text: Ones: 9 + 6 = 15. Write 5. Carry 1 to the tens.
Tens: 7 + 8 + 1 = 16. Write 6. Carry 1 to the hundreds.
Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

slides.tip: Write the little 1 on top of the next column. Then add it in!

notes.do: Work it on the whiteboard. Write the carried 1s in the second marker color.
notes.say: Ones first, then tens, then hundreds. Always right to left.
notes.ask: Why can't we write 15 in the ones place?
notes.listen: Only one digit fits in a place. 15 ones is 1 ten and 5 ones, so we regroup.

slides.title: Subtract with regrouping
slides.text: If the top digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next place.

steps.text: Ones: 1 − 6? Too small. Borrow 1 ten. Now 11 − 6 = 5. The tens go from 5 to 4.
Tens: 4 − 7? Too small. Borrow 1 hundred. Now 14 − 7 = 7. The hundreds go from 4 to 3.
A 0 on top? 500 − 237: borrow from the hundreds first. 5 hundreds become 4, and the 0 tens become 10. Then borrow 1 ten. The answer is 263.

slides.tip: Never flip the digits! 1 − 6 is NOT 6 − 1.

notes.do: Work 451 − 176 on the whiteboard. Cross out and rewrite each borrowed digit. Then show 500 − 237 slowly.
notes.ask: How can you check a subtraction answer?
notes.listen: Add the answer to the number you took away. You should get the top number back.

slides.title: Week 3 on paper
slides.text: Stack each one on paper. Then type.

items.why: Ones: 9 + 6 = 15. Write 5, carry 1. Tens: 7 + 4 + 1 = 12. Write 2, carry 1. Hundreds: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5. 525
items.no: Start with the ones. If a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry the 1 to the next column.

items.why: Ones: 4 − 8? Too small. Borrow 1 ten: 3 tens become 2, and 4 ones become 14 ones. 14 − 8 = 6. Tens: 2 − 5? Too small. Borrow 1 hundred: 6 hundreds become 5, and 2 tens become 12. 12 − 5 = 7. Hundreds: 5 − 2 = 3. 376
items.no: Start with the ones. If the top digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next place. Never flip the digits.
items.hint: Ones first: 4 − 8? You need to borrow.

items.why: Ones: 0 − 6? Too small. The tens place has 0, so first take 1 hundred: 7 hundreds become 6, and 0 tens become 10 tens. Now take 1 ten: 10 tens become 9, and 0 ones become 10 ones. 10 − 6 = 4. Tens: 9 − 4 = 5. Hundreds: 6 − 3 = 3. 354
items.no: Start with the ones. If the top digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next place. Never flip the digits.
items.hint: Ones first: 0 − 6? You need to borrow.

notes.do: Hands off. She does each one on paper. Praise every correct column out loud.
notes.ask: On 700 − 346, where do you borrow from first?
notes.listen: The hundreds, because the tens place has 0. 7 hundreds become 6, the tens become 10, then 9. Answer 354. If she writes 446 (she flipped the digits instead of borrowing), go back to the ones.

slides.title: Word problems and estimates
slides.text: Find the clue words. They tell you to add or subtract.

visual.text: ➕ or ➖ ?
visual.sub: Add: in all, altogether, total. Subtract: left, how many more, difference.

steps.text: “A shelf has 236 books. The library gets 187 more. How many books in all?” In all means add: 236 + 187 = 423.
“There are 450 pencils. Kids use 176. How many are left?” Left means subtract: 450 − 176 = 274.
Estimate: round each number to the nearest hundred. Then add. 236 → 200. 187 → 200. 200 + 200 = 400.
423 is close to 400. So 423 is a reasonable answer.

slides.tip: “How many more” means subtract. Find the difference.

notes.do: She underlines the clue word in each story on the whiteboard.
notes.ask: When you estimate 236 + 187, do you add 236 + 187?
notes.listen: No. You add the ROUNDED numbers: 200 + 200 = 400. The Checkpoint asks for estimates, and adding the exact numbers is the most common mistake.

slides.title: Add or subtract?
slides.text: Tap a card. Then tap Add or Subtract. Look for the clue words.

items.text: Wren has 125 stickers. She gets 140 more. How many in all?
items.why: “In all” means put together: add.

items.text: A bus has 48 seats. 29 are taken. How many are left?
items.why: “Left” means take away: subtract.
items.hint: Find the clue word at the end.

items.text: Liam read 214 pages. Mia read 186 pages. How many pages altogether?
items.why: “Altogether” means add.
items.hint: Are we putting the pages together?

items.text: Jen has 418 beads. Remy has 263. How many more does Jen have?
items.why: “How many more” means find the difference: subtract.

items.text: A farm has 156 hens and 238 ducks. What is the total?
items.why: “Total” means add.

items.text: There were 300 cups. Kids used 145. How many cups remain?
items.why: “Remain” means what is left: subtract.

slides.done: Add: in all, altogether, total. Subtract: left, remain, how many more.

notes.do: She reads each card out loud and says the clue word BEFORE she taps.
notes.listen: No. “She gets 140 more” is add, but “how many MORE does Jen have” is subtract (compare). Read the whole question.

slides.title: Week 4 on paper
slides.text: Underline the clue word on paper. Then solve.

items.q: The library has 318 kids' books and 275 grown-up books. How many books altogether?
items.why: Ones: 8 + 5 = 13. Write 3, carry 1. Tens: 1 + 7 + 1 = 9. Hundreds: 3 + 2 = 5. 593
items.no: Start with the ones. If a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry the 1 to the next column.

items.q: A jar had 605 beads. Nell used 248. How many beads are left?
items.why: Ones: 5 − 8? Too small. The tens place has 0, so first take 1 hundred: 6 hundreds become 5, and 0 tens become 10 tens. Now take 1 ten: 10 tens become 9, and 5 ones become 15 ones. 15 − 8 = 7. Tens: 9 − 4 = 5. Hundreds: 5 − 2 = 3. 357
items.no: Start with the ones. If the top digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next place. Never flip the digits.
items.hint: Ones first: 5 − 8? You need to borrow.

items.q: Estimate 381 + 442. Round each number to the nearest hundred first. Then add. Estimate: ____
items.no: Round each number to the nearest hundred first. Then add the rounded numbers. Do not add the exact numbers.

notes.do: She says the clue word out loud before she computes.
notes.listen: 400 (the tens digit is 8). 442 rounds to 400. Estimate 800.

slides.title: The shape of a story
slides.text: Most stories have the same shape.

visual.text: Problem → Try → Fix

steps.text: Character: who the story is about. Setting: where and when it happens.
Conflict: the problem. Attempt: a try to fix it. Resolution: how it gets fixed.
Sequence: beginning, middle, end. First, next, then and last are transition words.
Plot is what happens. Theme is the lesson. Ask: what did the character learn?

slides.tip: A theme must match what really happens in the story.

notes.do: Write PROBLEM → TRY → FIX on the whiteboard. Leave it up for the next slides.
notes.say: This is Theo's story shape too: missing sign, compass, Lookout Peak.
notes.ask: What is the difference between plot and theme?
notes.listen: Plot is what happens (Theo shared a marshmallow). Theme is the lesson (sharing with someone you love feels good).

slides.title: Zuri's Red Kite
slides.text: Read it out loud. Highlight the problem in one color.

visual.text:
Zuri's Red Kite
It was a windy Saturday at the park by the lake. Zuri had a new red kite. First, Grandpa helped her unroll the string. Next, Zuri ran, and the kite flew up high. Then a big gust of wind blew the kite into a tall oak tree! Zuri jumped for the string, but it was too high. She wanted to cry. “Let's stop and think,” said Grandpa. Zuri took a slow, deep breath. She gave the string a soft tug, then another. The kite wiggled free and floated down. Last, they flew it again, far away from the trees.

items.q: What is the setting?
choices: Zuri's school yard on a rainy Saturday
A park by the lake on a windy Saturday
Grandpa's backyard on a calm, quiet night
A sandy beach by the lake on a hot summer day
items.why: The story says “a windy Saturday at the park by the lake.” That is where and when.
no: The story is at a park, and it is windy, not rainy.
They are at the park, in the day, and it is windy.
There is a lake, but they are at a park, not a beach.

items.q: What is the conflict? The kite got stuck in a tall oak ____.
items.why: The kite stuck in the tree is Zuri's problem: the conflict.
items.no: Look at the sentence that starts with “Then.”

items.q: What was Zuri's first attempt, the one that did NOT work?
choices: She gave the string soft tugs
Grandpa climbed the tree
She jumped for the string
She bought a new kite
items.why: She jumped for the string, but it was too high. That try did not work.
no: That was her second try, and it worked.
Grandpa never climbs. He says, “Let's stop and think.”
She never buys a new kite.

items.q: What is the theme?
choices: A red kite can fly higher than a tall oak tree
Never fly a kite at the park when it is windy
When you have a problem, stay calm and think
Grandpas should climb trees to get kites down
items.why: Zuri stopped, took a breath and thought. Then she fixed it. The lesson: stay calm and think.
no: That is about the kite. It is not a lesson for people.
Zuri fixed the problem and flew it again. The story does not teach that.
Grandpa never climbs. He says, “Let's stop and think.”

notes.do: She reads it aloud. She highlights the conflict. Then she points to PROBLEM → TRY → FIX on the whiteboard and fills it in for Zuri.
notes.ask: What clue shows Zuri was upset?
notes.listen: “She wanted to cry.” That is a clue to her feelings, an inference.

slides.title: Put Zuri's story in order
slides.text: Tap the events in the order they happened.
steps: Grandpa helped Zuri unroll the string.
Wind blew the kite into a tree.
Zuri took a slow, deep breath.
slides.why: First the string, next the kite flew, then the tree, then the breath, and last the kite came down.
slides.hint: Look for first, next, then and last in the story.

notes.do: She finds each transition word in the story first, then taps.
notes.ask: Which words in the story told you the order?
notes.listen: First, Next, Then, Last. Those are transition words.

slides.title: Words from memory
slides.text: No peeking. Type the word.

items.q: When you trade 10 ones for 1 ten, you ____.
items.why: That is to regroup.
items.no: It starts with r-e.
items.hint: It is one of our six words.

items.q: A close guess made by rounding first is an ____.
items.why: That is an estimate.
items.no: It starts with e-s-t.

items.q: The lesson or big idea a story teaches is the ____.
items.why: That is the theme.
items.no: It starts with t-h.

notes.do: If she misses a word, she says it three times, spells it out loud, then types it again.

slides.title: Your Checkpoint game plan
slides.text: You reviewed all four weeks. You are ready!

steps.text: Math: work on paper first. Ones first. Regroup when you need to.
Word problems: find the clue word. Estimate means round first.
Reading: problem → try → fix. First, next, then, last. Theme = the lesson.
This week: the after-class lesson tonight. Then Practice and the Packet. The Checkpoint is on Sunday.

slides.tip: Only your first try earns points on the Checkpoint. Slow and right beats fast and wrong.

notes.do: Open her course page together. Read the task list one day at a time. She takes her 6 index cards home.
notes.say: Tonight: the after-class lesson and Show What You Know. Sunday: the real Checkpoint. Print the Pre/Post sheet first.
notes.ask: What will you do before you type every math answer?

slides.title: Checkpoint Review: On Your Own
slides.text: In class we reviewed Weeks 1 to 4. Now you practice on your own. Keep paper and a pencil next to you.

slides.title: Theo's stories out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or out loud to yourself.
prompts: What was Theo's conflict on his first hike? How did he fix it?
Tell what Theo's family did at the campsite. Use first, next, then and last.
What is the theme of the marshmallow story?

slides.title: Theo's trail story map
slides.text: Read Theo's four stories. The Checkpoint asks about them.

steps.text: Week 1: Theo's First Hike. Theo's first real hike. A forest trail on a misty, early morning. He brought his father's old brass compass.
Week 2: The Missing Sign. The trail split in two, and the sign was gone. That was the conflict. He used his compass and his map. He went right and reached Lookout Peak.
Week 3: Camping. Theo, Dad and his little sister Mia went camping. First the tent, next the fire, then chili. Last, they looked at the stars.
Week 4: The Last Marshmallow. One marshmallow was left. Theo broke it in half. He gave Mia the bigger piece. The theme: sharing with someone you love can feel better than keeping it.

slides.tip: Character and setting, problem → try → fix, sequence and theme. Theo's stories have them all!

slides.title: Review your words
slides.text: Say the meaning out loud first. Then flip the card to check.

words.meaning: What a digit is worth because of where it sits in a number.
words.example: In 862, the 8 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 800.

words.meaning: To trade 10 of one place for 1 of the next place.
A close guess. You round the numbers first.
The problem a character has in a story.
words.example: Zuri's kite is stuck in a tree. That is the conflict.

words.meaning: The order that things happen in.
words.example: First, next, then and last show the sequence.

words.meaning: The lesson or big idea a story teaches.
words.example: Zuri's story theme: stay calm and think when you have a problem.

slides.title: One rule for each week
slides.text: Read each rule out loud.

visual.text: Paper first!

steps.text: Week 1: a digit's place tells its value. To round, look one place to the right. 5 or more rounds up.
Week 2: compare the hundreds first. If they tie, look at the tens.
Week 3: ones first. Regroup when a column makes 10 or more. Borrow when the top digit is too small.
Week 4: find the clue word. To estimate, round first, then add.
Reading: character and setting. Problem → try → fix. First, next, then, last. Theme = the lesson.

slides.title: Weeks 1 and 2
slides.text: Work on paper. Then type.

items.q: In 258, what is the 5 worth?
items.why: The 5 is in the tens place. 5 tens = 50.
items.no: Is the 5 in the hundreds, tens or ones place?
items.hint: The 2 is worth 200. The 5 comes next.

items.q: Round 731 to the nearest hundred: ____
items.why: 731 is between 700 and 800. Look at the tens digit: 3. That is 4 or less, so round down. 700
items.no: Look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: 731 is between 700 and 800. Which one is it closer to?

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 0 and 9. 9 is bigger, so 490 is bigger. 409 < 490 means 409 is less than 490. <
items.no: Start with the hundreds. If they tie, look at the tens. The open side faces the bigger number.
items.hint: The point of the sign touches the smaller number.

slides.title: Week 3: regroup
slides.text: Stack each one on paper. Ones first.

items.why: Ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write 2, carry 1. Tens: 6 + 8 + 1 = 15. Write 5, carry 1. Hundreds: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. 752
items.no: Start with the ones. If a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry the 1 to the next column.

items.why: Ones: 3 − 6? Too small. Borrow 1 ten: 1 tens become 0, and 3 ones become 13 ones. 13 − 6 = 7. Tens: 0 − 5? Too small. Borrow 1 hundred: 7 hundreds become 6, and 0 tens become 10. 10 − 5 = 5. Hundreds: 6 − 4 = 2. 257
items.no: Start with the ones. If the top digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next place. Never flip the digits.
items.hint: Ones first: 3 − 6? You need to borrow.

items.why: Ones: 0 − 4? Too small. The tens place has 0, so first take 1 hundred: 6 hundreds become 5, and 0 tens become 10 tens. Now take 1 ten: 10 tens become 9, and 0 ones become 10 ones. 10 − 4 = 6. Tens: 9 − 7 = 2. Hundreds: 5 − 2 = 3. 326
items.no: Start with the ones. If the top digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next place. Never flip the digits.
items.hint: Ones first: 0 − 4? You need to borrow.

slides.title: Week 4: word problems
slides.text: Find the clue word. Then solve on paper.

items.q: The Sharks sold 168 hot dogs and 254 drinks at the game. How many things did they sell in all?
items.why: Ones: 8 + 4 = 12. Write 2, carry 1. Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12. Write 2, carry 1. Hundreds: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. 422
items.no: Start with the ones. If a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry the 1 to the next column.

items.q: Estimate 147 + 362. Round each number to the nearest hundred first. Then add. Estimate: ____
items.no: Round each number to the nearest hundred first. Then add the rounded numbers. Do not add the exact numbers.

items.q: Kiara has 652 shells. Jude has 375 shells. How many more shells does Kiara have?
items.why: “How many more” means subtract: 652 − 375. Ones: 2 − 5? Borrow: 12 − 5 = 7. Tens: 4 − 7? Borrow: 14 − 7 = 7. Hundreds: 5 − 3 = 2. 277
no: 1027 is 652 + 375. “How many more” means subtract.
Did you forget that the 6 hundreds became 5? Cross it out when you borrow.
Did you flip 2 − 5 into 5 − 2? Borrow instead: 12 − 5 = 7.

slides.title: Plot or theme?
slides.text: Tap a card. Is it plot (what happens) or theme (the lesson)?

items.text: Theo broke the marshmallow in half.
items.why: That is something that happens: plot.
items.hint: Is it an event or a lesson?

items.text: Sharing with someone you love can feel good.
items.why: That is a lesson about life: theme.
items.hint: Could this lesson fit your own life?

items.text: Zuri's kite got stuck in a tree.
items.why: That is an event in the story: plot.
items.hint: Did it happen in the story?

items.text: Stay calm and think when you have a problem.
items.why: That is a lesson: theme.

items.text: The family cooked chili over the fire.
items.why: That happens in the story: plot.

items.text: Being brave means you try, even when you are scared.
items.why: That is a big idea about life: theme.

slides.done: Plot = what happens. Theme = the lesson the story teaches.

slides.title: Dante's Big Game
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text:
Dante's Big Game
It was the last soccer game of the fall at Oak Park. Dante's team, the Sharks, was tied with the Hawks. Dante wanted to score the winning goal. First, he kicked the ball hard, but it flew past the net. Next, he tried again and missed. Dante's face felt hot. Then he saw his friend Lia, all alone by the net. Dante passed the ball to her. Lia kicked it in. Goal! The Sharks won! Last, the whole team cheered, and Lia hugged Dante. “That was the best pass ever,” she said.

items.q: Who is the main character? Type the name.
items.why: The story is mostly about Dante.
items.no: Whose story is it? Look at the title.

items.q: What is Dante's conflict?
choices: His friend Lia is playing for the other team
He wants to score, but he keeps missing
The game is canceled because of the rain
He cannot find his soccer ball before the game
items.why: He wants the winning goal, but his first two kicks miss. That is his problem.

teacher.objective: Ce'Line reviews all of Unit 1 (Pathways Weeks 1–4) so she can pass the Pathways Week 5 Checkpoint: Unit 1 Review with 85 or more. No new skill. Math: place value, expanded form and rounding to the nearest ten and hundred (Week 1); comparing with >, <, = and ordering 3-digit numbers, including races where the smallest time wins (Week 2); adding and subtracting with regrouping, including a 0 in the tens (Week 3); clue words in word problems and estimating by rounding to the nearest hundred (Week 4). Reading: Theo's four trail stories retold; character and setting, conflict → attempt → resolution, sequence with transition words, and plot vs. theme, practiced on a new story (Zuri's Red Kite). Six Checkpoint words: place value, regroup, estimate, conflict, sequence, theme.
materials: The class lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Whiteboard and two marker colors (one color only for carried and borrowed numbers)
6 index cards (Word Power; she writes the backs at home)
A highlighter (Zuri's conflict) and pencil and paper
Packet (2 pages), printed for her to take home: page 1 Thursday, page 2 Friday

plan.do: Class slide 1. Review day, no new skill. She names one thing she remembers; write it on the board.
Class slide 2. She retells Theo's four stories. Draw the 4-stop trail on the whiteboard (Hike, Missing Sign, Camping, Marshmallow) and add a word at each stop.
Class slide 3. Four weeks, eight skills. She names her easiest and hardest week.
Class slide 4. Six words, read aloud, said in her own words. She writes each on an index card.
Class slides 5–6. 862 in a place value chart; expanded form; round to the nearest ten and hundred. Then 491, 705 and 765 on paper.
Class slides 7–8. 746 vs 764; order 391, 319, 913; races. Then 508 ___ 580, greatest to least, and the fastest runner.
Class slides 12–14. Clue words; 236 + 187 and the estimate 400. Sort six stories into Add or Subtract. Then two word problems and estimate 381 + 442.
Class slide 15. PROBLEM → TRY → FIX on the whiteboard; sequence words; plot vs. theme.
Class slide 16. She reads aloud and highlights the conflict. Setting, conflict, first attempt, theme.
Class slide 17. She finds First, Next, Then, Last in the story, then puts five events in order.
Class slide 18. Regroup, estimate, theme, typed with no peeking.
Class slide 19. The Checkpoint game plan. Read the task list on the course page; the Checkpoint is Sunday.

watch: Confidence first: she has struggled on Pathways, so praise each correct column and each correct story answer out loud. If she freezes, do the first step together and let her finish.

Rounding (Week 1): to the nearest hundred, look at the TENS digit; to the nearest ten, look at the ONES digit. The usual slip is looking at the wrong digit (765 → she says 770 instead of 800 when asked for the nearest hundred).
Comparing (Week 2): hundreds first, then tens. Watch the direction of > and <: the open side faces the bigger number. In races and times, the SMALLEST number wins.

Regrouping (Week 3): she may forget to add the carried 1, or flip the digits when subtracting (1 − 6 written as 6 − 1, so 451 − 176 becomes 325). A 0 in the tens (500 − 237, 700 − 346) means borrowing from the hundreds first. Have her check subtraction by adding.

Word problems (Week 4): “in all, altogether, total” = add; “left, remain, how many more, difference” = subtract. “More” alone is not always add. On estimate questions she must add the ROUNDED numbers (the Checkpoint asks for 700 for 264 + 419, not 683).

Reading: conflict = the problem, attempt = a try, resolution = the fix. Theme is a lesson about life, not an event; a theme must match what happens. The Checkpoint asks many questions about Theo's stories, so the story talk matters.

On the Checkpoint: 2 tries per question, and only the first try earns points. It wants single words for the vocabulary blanks (regroup, borrow, carry, estimate, theme, conflict, sequence, plot, resolution, infer). She works every math problem on paper and compares her paper to the screen before pressing Check.

The Checkpoint (Pathways Week 5) checks Weeks 1–4 math and reading, asks many recall questions about Theo's stories (the compass, Lookout Peak, the grandfather's valley view, tent first, chili, the stars, the marshmallow broken in half for Mia), and the vocabulary words regroup, borrow, carry, estimate, conflict, attempt, resolution, setting, sequence, transition words, theme, plot and infer. None of our questions copy the Checkpoint's. Before class, check her Lesson 4 Show What You Know score; if it is under 85, spend 2 extra minutes on Week 4 (clue words and estimating). Tonight she does the after-class lesson (about 25 minutes); it ends with Show What You Know (8 questions: 4 math and 4 reading, one per Week 1–4 skill; 3 different sets for retakes; she needs 7 of 8 for 85). Each question is labeled Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4 or Week N reading, so the Formspree missed list shows which week to reteach. The Checkpoint is on her task list for Sunday, after Practice and both Packet pages; she prints the Pre/Post sheet from the Checkpoint's first page and does page 1 first. If her Checkpoint score is under 85, her Monday task is to redo the matching part of the after-class lesson and retake it (it gives fresh questions, up to 3 attempts). Look at her Checkpoint score at the start of Lesson 6. The Science and Social Studies Week 5 Checkpoints and both Florida Focus 1 lessons are optional and self-paced; you do not teach them.

tasks: Tuesday (after class): do the after-class lesson. It ends with Show What You Know. Aim for 85.
Wednesday: do the Practice set. Work every math problem on paper first.
Thursday: print the Packet and do page 1. Then write the meaning on the back of each of your 6 word cards.
Saturday: do the Practice set again. You get new questions.
Sunday: do the Pathways Unit 1 Checkpoint. First print the Pre/Post sheet and do page 1. Work every math problem on paper. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111.

Monday: if your Checkpoint score is under 85, go back to the after-class lesson and redo the part that was hard. Then retake the Checkpoint. It gives you new questions. If you got 85 or more, take Monday off! Optional: try a Science or Social Studies Checkpoint from the list below.
